summary: Describes the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm, which translates IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers, including ICMP. It is a proposed standard, obsoletes RFC 2765, and was replaced by RFC 7915.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines a box that sits between an old IPv4 network and a new IPv6 one and rewrites the addresses on packets as they pass, so the two worlds can talk without either side changing. It also says how to translate the error and control messages that go with them.

questions: how does ipv4 to ipv6 translation work
what is the difference between stateless and stateful translation
how are icmp messages translated between ipv4 and ipv6
subtitle: The rules for rewriting packet headers so that an IPv4 network and an IPv6 network can talk to each other.

tldr.problem: Hosts that speak only IPv4 and hosts that speak only IPv6 cannot reach each other, and there was no agreed way to rewrite one protocol's packets into the other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a stateless translator, an XLAT, that replaces the IPv4 or IPv6 header with the other one, rewrites the addresses algorithmically, and translates the ICMP control messages alongside them.
tldr.outcome: It obsoleted RFC 2765, and was itself later obsoleted by RFC 7915 and updated by RFC 6791 and RFC 7757, so it is no longer the current statement of the algorithm.

facts.label: Hosts handling a Packet Too Big of 1280

today: RFC 6145 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2011, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 7915 and updated by RFC 6791 and RFC 7757. It itself obsoleted RFC 2765.

sections.title: What the Translator Does
sections.content:
RFC 6145 describes the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm, SIIT, which translates between IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers, including ICMP headers. It obsoletes RFC 2765 and comes out of the 2008 to 2010 effort to define a replacement for NAT-PT, which was given Historic status when RFC 4966 was published in 2007. Readers are expected to have read the framework in RFC 6144, and implementations of this specification must also support the address translation algorithms in RFC 6052, and may also support the stateful translation in RFC 6146.

The translation model has two or more network domains connected by one or more IP/ICMP translators, called XLATs. The assumptions behind both modes of operation are the same: a system with an IPv4 address but no IPv6 address is talking to a system with an IPv6 address but no IPv4 address, or the two systems have no contiguous routing connectivity and so their traffic has to be translated.

In the stateless mode, a specific IPv6 address range represents the IPv4 systems, giving IPv4-converted addresses, and the IPv6 systems have IPv4-translatable addresses that can be mapped algorithmically to a subset of the service provider's IPv4 addresses. There is generally no need to think about translation tables, because the IPv4 and IPv6 counterparts are algorithmically related. In the stateful mode, the same IPv6 range represents the IPv4 systems, but the IPv6 systems may use any IPv6 addresses outside that range, and a translation table is then needed to bind their addresses to the IPv4 addresses the translator holds. The address mechanisms for both are defined in RFC 6052.

There are limits. The translating function does not translate any IPv4 options, and does not translate IPv6 extension headers other than the Fragment Header. Fragmented IPv4 UDP packets without a UDP checksum are not of significant use on the internet and will generally not be translated, though they are when the translator is configured to forward packets without a checksum. Fragmented ICMP and ICMPv6 packets will not be translated at all. The header translation is consistent with the requirements of multicast IP and ICMP headers, but IPv4 multicast addresses cannot be mapped to IPv6 multicast addresses using the unicast mapping rule.

Packet size is the last piece of the background. The IPv4 and IPv6 headers are 20 or more octets and 40 octets respectively, so handling the maximum packet size is critical. There are three mechanisms: path MTU discovery, fragmentation, and transport-layer negotiation such as the TCP Maximum Segment Size option. The translator must behave as a router, meaning it must send a Packet Too Big error message or fragment the packet when the packet size exceeds the MTU of the next-hop interface.

sections.title: Translating IPv4 into IPv6
sections.content:
When a translator receives an IPv4 datagram addressed towards the IPv6 domain, it replaces the IPv4 header with an IPv6 header, updates the transport checksum where the transport is supported, leaves the data portion untouched, and forwards the packet based on the new IPv6 destination address.

Fragmentation and path MTU discovery come first, because the IPv6 header is larger. Path MTU discovery is mandatory in IPv6 and optional in IPv4, and IPv6 routers never fragment a packet, only the sender can. When an IPv4 node performs path MTU discovery by setting the Don't Fragment bit, the discovery can operate end to end across the translator, and either IPv4 or IPv6 routers might send Packet Too Big messages back. An IPv6 Fragment Header is therefore only included if the IPv4 packet is already fragmented. When the IPv4 sender does not set the Don't Fragment bit, the translator must make sure the packet does not exceed the path MTU on the IPv6 side, by fragmenting the IPv4 packet so it fits in 1280-byte IPv6 packets, which is the minimum IPv6 MTU. The RFC notes that the Fragment Header has caused operational difficulties in practice because of limited firewall support, and allows a configuration function to adjust the assumed minimum IPv6 MTU to the real value, so that the Fragment Header is included less often. When the sender has not set the bit, the translator should always include a Fragment Header to signal that the sender allows fragmentation.

The header fields themselves are set as follows. The version becomes 6. The traffic class is copied from the IPv4 Type of Service octet by default, though an implementation should offer an administratively configurable option to ignore the IPv4 value and always set the traffic class to zero. The flow label is zero. The payload length is the IPv4 total length minus the size of the IPv4 header and any IPv4 options. The next header is the IPv4 protocol number, except that ICMPv4, protocol 1, becomes ICMPv6, protocol 58. The hop limit is derived from the IPv4 TTL, and since the translator is a router it must decrement one or the other and check for zero, sending the relevant error. The source address is the IPv4-converted address derived from the IPv4 source, and an illegal source address such as 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1 should be silently dropped. The destination address in stateless mode is the IPv4-translatable address derived from the IPv4 destination; in stateful mode it comes from the Binding Information Bases reflecting the session state in the translator.

IPv4 options must be ignored and the packet translated normally, except that an unexpired source route option means the packet must be discarded and an ICMPv4 Destination Unreachable, Source Route Failed error returned. If a Fragment Header has to be added, the payload length gains 8 bytes, the next header becomes the Fragment Header, protocol 44, the fragment offset and More Fragments bit are copied, and the low-order 16 bits of the IPv4 identification are carried across with the high-order bits set to zero. The translator should make sure that packets belonging to the same flow leave it in the order they arrived.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator swaps the header for the larger IPv6 one, rewrites the two addresses, and copies most of the other fields across. The awkward part is size: if the original packet did not say it was too big to fragment, the translator has to split it itself.

sections.title: Translating IPv6 into IPv4
sections.content:
In the other direction, the translator replaces the IPv6 header with an IPv4 header. Because the ICMPv6, TCP, UDP and DCCP headers carry checksums that cover the IP header, if the address mapping is not checksum neutral the checksum must be evaluated before translation and the ICMP and transport-layer headers updated. The data portion is left unchanged and the packet is forwarded on the new IPv4 destination.

Fragmentation and the minimum link MTU differ between the two protocols: an IPv6 link must have an MTU of 1280 bytes or greater, while the corresponding IPv4 limit is 68 bytes. Path MTU discovery across a translator relies on ICMP Packet Too Big messages being received and processed by IPv6 hosts. Where an ICMPv4 Packet Too Big is translated into an ICMPv6 one and is correctly handled by the IPv6 hosts, the translator can rely on those hosts sending later packets with IPv6 Fragment Headers, and it should then generate the IPv4 packet with a cleared Don't Fragment bit and the identification value from the IPv6 Fragment Header. Where the ICMPv4 message is filtered or mishandled, the IPv6 host will never generate a Fragment Header, and the translator should set the IPv4 Don't Fragment bit instead. The RFC says that although setting that bit may create PMTUD black holes on IPv4 links smaller than 1260 octets, that is safer than causing IPv4 reassembly errors.

The header fields are set as follows. The version becomes 4 and the header length is 5, with no IPv4 options. The type of service octet is copied from the IPv6 traffic class by default, though an implementation should be able to ignore it and always set a specified value. The total length is the IPv6 payload length plus the size of the IPv4 header. The identification is all zero, though the translator may be given a function to generate it for packets larger than 88 bytes and no larger than 1280 bytes, to avoid black holes caused by ICMPv4 filtering. The More Fragments flag is zero and the Don't Fragment flag is one, again with an option to clear the latter for packets in that size range. The fragment offset is all zeros. The time to live comes from the IPv6 hop limit, decremented by the translator as any router would. For the protocol field, the IPv6 Fragment header is handled as described below, ICMPv6 becomes ICMPv4, and the Hop-by-Hop, Routing and Destination Options headers are skipped over, since they have no meaning in IPv4; the first next header that matches none of those has its value copied into the protocol field, so all transport protocols are translated. The header checksum is computed once the header exists. The source address is derived from the IPv6 source in stateless mode, and a packet whose source is not an IPv4-translatable address should be dropped with an ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable error when the translator is stateless only; an illegal source address such as ::1 should be silently dropped. The destination address is derived from the IPv6 destination. A routing header with a non-zero Segments Left field means the packet must not be translated, and an ICMPv6 Parameter Problem error should be returned pointing at the first byte of that field.

When there is a Fragment Header, the total length loses the 8 bytes of that header and gains the size of the IPv4 header, the identification is copied from the low-order 16 bits of the Fragment Header's identification field, the More Fragments flag is copied from the M flag, the Don't Fragment flag is cleared so IPv4 routers may fragment further, and the fragment offset is copied. If a translated packet with the Don't Fragment bit set would be larger than the MTU of the next-hop interface, the translator must drop it and send an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message with an adjusted MTU.
sections.plainLanguage: Going the other way is similar but the header is smaller, so the sizes work in the translator's favour. The one judgement call is whether to mark the packet as already too big to fragment, which depends on whether the far end is likely to be handling Packet Too Big messages properly.

sections.title: Translating ICMP
sections.content:
All ICMPv4 messages that are translated need the ICMPv6 checksum calculated, because ICMPv6, unlike ICMPv4, has a pseudo-header checksum like UDP and TCP. The type must always be translated, and for error messages the included IP header must also be translated.

For the query messages, Echo and Echo Reply, types 8 and 0, become types 128 and 129, with the checksum adjusted for the type change and for the pseudo-header. Information Request and Reply, Timestamp and Timestamp Reply, and Address Mask Request and Reply are all obsoleted in ICMPv6 and are silently dropped. Router Advertisement and Router Solicitation are single-hop messages and are silently dropped, as are unknown ICMPv4 types. The ordinary IGMP messages are single-hop and should be silently dropped too, as should the others that multicast routing protocols might use, since having router adjacencies across a translator would be a configuration error.

For the error messages, Destination Unreachable becomes ICMPv6 type 1, with the code translated: codes 0 and 1 become code 0, no route to destination; code 2, protocol unreachable, becomes an ICMPv6 Parameter Problem with the pointer aimed at the IPv6 Next Header field; code 3, port unreachable, becomes code 4; code 4, fragmentation needed with DF set, becomes an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big with code 0 and an MTU adjusted for the difference between the header sizes, namely the minimum of the advertised MTU plus 20, the MTU of the IPv6 next hop, and the MTU of the IPv4 next hop plus 20; and if the IPv4 router set the MTU field to zero because it does not implement RFC 1191, the translator must use the plateau values from that RFC to work out a likely path MTU. Codes 5, 6, 7, 8 and 11 become code 0, codes 9, 10, 13 and 15 become code 1, code 14 is silently dropped, and any other code is silently dropped.

Redirect, Alternative Host Address and Source Quench are silently dropped, the last because it is obsoleted in ICMPv6. Time Exceeded becomes type 3 with the code unchanged. Parameter Problem becomes type 4: code 0 keeps code 0 with the pointer rewritten, code 1 is silently dropped, and code 2 becomes code 0 with the pointer rewritten. Each of those rewrites uses a table that maps the byte offset of the offending field in the IPv4 header to the byte offset of the corresponding field in the IPv6 header.

ICMP error messages carry the packet that caused the error, and that inner packet must be translated just like a normal IP packet, with the outer header's total length updated if the length changes. The translation of the inner header stops at the first embedded header, and the packet is dropped if it contains more than one. If the received ICMP message carries an extension defined in RFC 4884, its length attribute must be adjusted, and it should be truncated if it exceeds the maximum ICMPv6 message size on the outgoing interface. Extensions not defined in that RFC are passed as opaque bit strings, so any IPv4 addresses inside them are not translated.
sections.plainLanguage: The control messages need their own translation tables, because IPv4 and IPv6 do not have the same set of error codes and some of the old ones have no equivalent at all. Anything with no equivalent is dropped quietly rather than passed on.

sections.title: The Packet Too Big Problem
sections.content:
Two studies of how IPv6-capable web servers on the internet behave found that approximately 95% responded as expected to an IPv6 Packet Too Big indicating an MTU of 1280, but only 43% responded as expected to one indicating an MTU below 1280, probably because of firewalls that violate the guidance in RFC 4890. Both failures, the 5% wrong response at 1280 and the 57% wrong response below it, cause PMTUD black holes. The translator cannot improve the first case, but it can improve the second, and there are two approaches that a translator should be able to be configured for.

The first approach constrains where the translator is deployed: four of the scenarios intended for stateless translators have no IPv6 hosts on the internet, and in those the IPv6 hosts, host-based firewalls and network firewalls can be administered to comply with RFC 4890 and so avoid the problem.

The second approach is needed when the translator does have IPv6 hosts or firewalls on the internet that do not comply with RFC 2460. In the IPv4-to-IPv6 direction, if the MTU in an ICMPv4 Packet Too Big is below 1280 the translator changes it to 1280, which is meant to make the IPv6 host and firewall process the message and send later packets with an IPv6 Fragment Header. In the IPv6-to-IPv4 direction, if there is a Fragment Header the last 16 bits of its value must be used for the IPv4 identification value. If there is no Fragment Header and the packet is 1280 bytes or less, the translator should set the Don't Fragment bit to zero and generate an IPv4 identification value, and to avoid the problems described in RFC 4963 it is recommended that the translator keep three-tuple state for generating that value. If the packet is larger than 1280 bytes, the translator should set the IPv4 Don't Fragment bit.
sections.plainLanguage: Many hosts ignore a Packet Too Big message that says the packet must be smaller than the IPv6 minimum, and that silently breaks path MTU discovery. The RFC gives the translator a way to paper over it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using stateless IP/ICMP translators does not introduce new security issues beyond those already present in IPv4 and IPv6 and in the routing protocols used to get packets to the translator. There are potential issues in deriving an IPv4 address from an IPv6 address, particularly for addresses like broadcast or loopback addresses and for IPv6 addresses that are not IPv4-translatable, and RFC 6052 addresses those.

As with IPv4-to-IPv4 network address translation, the IPsec Authentication Header cannot be used across an IPv6-to-IPv4 translator. As with IPv4-to-IPv4 translation, packets with tunnel mode Encapsulating Security Payload can be translated, because tunnel mode ESP does not depend on header fields before the ESP header; transport mode ESP will fail with IPv6-to-IPv4 translation unless checksum-neutral addresses are used. In both cases the IPsec ESP endpoints will normally detect the presence of the translator and encapsulate ESP in UDP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new here, except that IPsec in transport mode cannot survive the crossing, and tunnel mode is fine because it does not look at the outer headers.
